Explanation: These are sites where mature lymphocytes encounter antigen and mount adaptive responses, rather than the primary sites of lymphocyte development.
Source Section: Lymphoid Tissue - primary versus secondary tissues; PDF p. 3
Notes: Verified: all four are secondary (peripheral) lymphoid organs (Chapel and Haeney, Essentials of Clinical Immunology 7e, 2023). Board overlap: do not pair on the same board with a primary-lymphoid category (bone marrow/thymus).

Connection Title: Findings of leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1
Explanation: Defective CD18-containing beta-2 integrins impair firm adhesion and tissue recruitment of leukocytes, producing this characteristic clinical pattern.
Source Section: Inflammation - disorders of leukocyte migration; PDF p. 18
Notes: Verified: ITGB2/CD18 beta-2 integrin defect; delayed cord separation, absent pus, impaired wound healing, defective firm adhesion are classic (Bonilla et al., JACI 2015;136:1186).

Explanation: LYST dysfunction causes abnormal lysosomal trafficking; the pigmentary, hematologic and neurologic findings together identify Chediak-Higashi syndrome.
Source Section: Inflammation - Chediak-Higashi syndrome; PDF p. 18
Notes: Verified: LYST mutation with partial albinism, giant granules, peripheral neuropathy (Bonilla et al., JACI 2015). Recurrent pyogenic infection is also characteristic but correctly not forced as a 4th tile.

Connection Title: Growth factors in inflammatory tissue repair
Explanation: These growth factors participate in repair after inflammation through angiogenesis, fibroblast recruitment or extracellular matrix deposition; their individual effects are not identical.
Source Section: Inflammation - chronic inflammatory response; PDF p. 19
Notes: Verified distinct roles: PDGF (fibroblast/smooth-muscle recruitment), TGF-beta (ECM/fibrosis), VEGF (angiogenesis), FGF (angiogenesis/fibroblast) (standard pathology references, e.g., Kumar, Robbins Basic Pathology 10e, 2018). Retain 'repair' wording; VEGF is not a collagen inducer. Board overlap: TGF-beta also anchors Treg group IMM-008.

Explanation: These cytokines are associated with Th2 responses; IL-4 and IL-13 support type 2 immunity, IL-5 supports eosinophils, and IL-10 has immunoregulatory effects.
Source Section: Cytokines - Th2 response; PDF p. 23
Notes: Core Th2 (type 2) cytokines IL-4/IL-5/IL-13 verified (Nakayama et al., Annu Rev Immunol 2017; Masopust et al., Guidelines for T cell nomenclature, Nat Rev Immunol 2026). Qualifier: IL-10 is historically Th2 but is now a broadly expressed regulatory cytokine (Rasquinha et al., J Immunol 2021); retain 'Th2-associated' wording. Board overlap: IL-10 also anchors Treg group IMM-008 - do not place both on one board.

Explanation: MHC class I molecules include beta-2 microglobulin and usually display intracellularly derived peptides to CD8 T cells; most nucleated cells express them.
Source Section: T-cells - MHC class I; PDF p. 27
Notes: Verified (Chapel and Haeney 2023). Qualifier: cross-presentation is the exception; retain 'usual/endogenous' wording.

Explanation: MHC class II typically presents endocytosed antigen to CD4 T cells. The invariant chain protects its peptide-binding groove during assembly; DP, DQ and DR encode class II molecules.
Source Section: T-cells - MHC class II; PDF p. 27
Notes: Verified: CD4, invariant chain (CD74), HLA-DP/DQ/DR, exogenous pathway (Chapel and Haeney 2023). Qualifier: autophagy can load endogenous peptides onto MHC II.

Explanation: Conventional regulatory T cells are characterized by FOXP3 and high CD25 expression and can suppress immune responses through mechanisms including IL-10 and TGF-beta.
Source Section: T-cells - regulatory T-cell activation; PDF p. 28
Notes: Verified: FOXP3 (lineage-defining), high CD25, IL-10 and TGF-beta suppression (Lu et al., Nat Rev Immunol 2017; Georgiev et al., J Clin Immunol 2019). None individually Treg-specific; the combination identifies Tregs. Board overlap: IL-10 shared with IMM-005, TGF-beta with IMM-004.

Connection Title: Surface molecules on mature naive B cells
Explanation: These surface molecules are expressed on mature naive B cells; MHC II enables presentation of processed antigen to helper T cells.
Source Section: B-cells - naive mature B-cell; PDF p. 31
Notes: Verified for mature naive B cells (Chapel and Haeney 2023). Qualifier: markers shift with differentiation (plasma cells lose CD19/CD20); MHC II is shared with other APCs - retain 'mature naive B cell' framing.

Explanation: B cells internalize protein antigen and present peptides through MHC II; helper T-cell interactions, including CD40L binding CD40, support the T-dependent antibody response.
Source Section: B-cells - Th-dependent activation; PDF p. 32
Notes: Verified (Chapel and Haeney 2023). Board overlap: MHC II shared with IMM-007/IMM-009; CD40-CD40L shared with IMM-025.

Explanation: IgG is the most abundant serum immunoglobulin, crosses the placenta and mediates opsonization; appropriate IgG subclasses can activate classical complement.
Source Section: Antibodies - IgG; PDF p. 37
Notes: Verified (Woof and Mestecky, Immunol Rev 2005). Qualifier: classical complement activation is subclass-dependent (IgG1/IgG3 strong, IgG2 weak, IgG4 poor) - do not imply all subclasses activate complement equally.

Explanation: Secretory IgA predominates at these mucosal/secretory sites and in breast milk, mediating mucosal and passive protection; tears are a canonical secretory-IgA fluid.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: IgA-associated secretions and tissue; secretory IgA sites
Source Section: Antibodies - IgA; PDF p. 37
Notes: REVISED: original tile 'Sweat' replaced with 'Tears.' Tears are a canonical secretory-IgA site (Woof and Mestecky, Immunol Rev 2005; Li et al., Biomed Res Int 2019); sweat IgA exists (Okada et al., J Invest Dermatol 1988) but is non-standard for boards. Original Bootcamp source cited only for breast milk, saliva and MALT; the tears replacement is supported by the added references.

Explanation: Secreted IgM is commonly pentameric with a J chain and is prominent early in a primary response; antigen-bound IgM efficiently activates classical complement.
Source Section: Antibodies - IgM; PDF p. 37
Notes: Verified (Woof and Mestecky 2005). Qualifier: membrane IgM is monomeric; 'pentamer' refers to the usual secreted form.

Explanation: IgE binds high-affinity receptors on mast cells; allergen crosslinking can trigger immediate hypersensitivity, while IgE also participates in defense against helminths.
Source Section: Antibodies - IgE; PDF p. 37
Notes: Verified: FcepsilonRI binding, allergen crosslinking triggers type I hypersensitivity, antihelminth role (Chapel and Haeney 2023).

Explanation: These proteins join C5b to build the membrane attack complex, the pore-forming terminal complement complex.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Proteins recruited to C5b; terminal/MAC components
Source Section: Complement - common pathway; PDF p. 41
Notes: Verified: C6-C9 are recruited to C5b to form MAC (C5b-9) (Chapel and Haeney 2023). Subset note: C5b is part of the complete complex but intentionally excluded; the title's 'later/terminal' wording is accurate.

Explanation: Hereditary C1-inhibitor deficiency causes excess bradykinin, reduced C4 and recurrent non-pitting edema that can involve the intestinal wall.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Hereditary angioedema due to C1-inhibitor deficiency
Source Section: Complement - C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency and case; PDF pp. 42-43
Notes: Verified: autosomal dominant SERPING1 deficiency, bradykinin excess, low C4, recurrent bowel-wall edema (Bonilla et al., JACI 2015). Qualifier: distinct from HAE with normal C1-INH (normal C4).

Explanation: Loss of GPI-anchored complement regulators causes complement-mediated hemolysis in PNH; unusual-site thrombosis, including hepatic venous thrombosis, is a characteristic association.
Source Section: Complement - paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria; PDF p. 42
Notes: Verified: PIGA-related loss of GPI-anchored CD55/CD59, Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria, atypical-site thrombosis incl hepatic vein/Budd-Chiari (Brodsky RA, Blood 2014;124:2804). Qualifier: 'can occur' findings, not obligatory.

Explanation: Each uses attenuated live virus to stimulate immunity. The MMR product contains three attenuated viruses; the other tiles each refer to a separate vaccine.
Source Section: Vaccinations - live attenuated examples; PDF p. 46
Notes: Verified live attenuated viral vaccines: MMR, varicella, rotavirus, yellow fever (Kelso et al., AAAAI Practice Parameter 2012; Pollard and Bijker, Nat Rev Immunol 2021).

Explanation: Each delivers protein antigen rather than a replicating organism: selected pertussis proteins, hepatitis B surface antigen, HPV capsid proteins, or inactivated tetanus toxin.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Vaccines using protein antigens; non-live protein/subunit and toxoid vaccines
Source Section: Vaccinations - subunit protein and toxoid vaccines; PDF p. 46
Notes: Verified (Pollard and Bijker, Nat Rev Immunol 2021): acellular pertussis (purified protein), recombinant HBsAg, HPV VLP, tetanus toxoid. 'Protein antigen' is the shared relationship; manufacturing method differs. Board overlap: HBV and HPV also appear in IMM-020 - do not place both connections on one board.

Explanation: Hepatitis A and Salk polio vaccines use inactivated virus; hepatitis B and HPV vaccines use recombinant viral proteins. All four are non-live viral vaccines.
Source Section: Vaccinations - whole inactivated and subunit protein examples; PDF p. 46
Notes: Verified (Pollard and Bijker 2021; Kelso et al. 2012): hep A and Salk/IPV inactivated; HBV and HPV recombinant - all non-live viral. Title correctly spans inactivated + recombinant. Board overlap: HBV/HPV shared with IMM-019.

Explanation: SCID disrupts T-cell development or function, often producing low TRECs, marked T-cell lymphopenia and early severe infections; lack of a thymic shadow is a classic supporting clue.
Source Section: Immunodeficiency Syndromes - SCID; PDF p. 49
Notes: Verified: low TRECs on newborn screening, absent thymic shadow, profound T-cell lymphopenia, early opportunistic infection (Bonilla et al., JACI 2015). Qualifier: B/NK-cell pattern varies by genotype - these are characteristic clues, not universal requirements.

Explanation: BTK-related failure of B-cell maturation produces very few mature B cells, deficient antibody production and small or absent lymphoid structures such as tonsils.
Source Section: Immunodeficiency Syndromes - Bruton agammaglobulinemia; PDF p. 49
Notes: Verified: BTK mutation, markedly reduced/absent mature B cells, panhypogammaglobulinemia, absent/small tonsils and lymph nodes (Bonilla et al., JACI 2015).

Explanation: DiGeorge-associated abnormal pharyngeal apparatus development can impair thymic and parathyroid development, linking T-cell deficiency to low PTH and hypocalcemia.
Source Section: Immunodeficiency Syndromes - thymic aplasia; PDF p. 49
Notes: Verified: 22q11.2 deletion, thymic hypoplasia/T-cell deficiency, hypoparathyroidism with low PTH and hypocalcemia (Mustillo et al., J Clin Immunol 2023). Qualifier: immune severity is a spectrum (complete aplasia is uncommon).

Tile 1: Low IgA with preserved IgG / IgM
Explanation: Selective IgA deficiency can compromise mucosal defense, interfere with IgA-based celiac testing and, in a small subset of patients, be associated with anaphylactic transfusion reactions involving anti-IgA antibodies.
Source Section: Immunodeficiency Syndromes - selective IgA deficiency; PDF p. 50
Notes: Verified: IgA <7 mg/dL with normal IgG/IgM; Giardia susceptibility; false-negative tTG-IgA requires IgG-based celiac testing (Rubio-Tapia et al., ACG 2023); anti-IgA anaphylactic transfusion reaction is a recognized but rare and debated association (Bonilla et al., JACI 2015; Soutar et al., Br J Haematol 2023). Keep 'can occur' framing for the transfusion tile.

Explanation: Deficient T-cell CD40 ligand impairs class switching and T-cell help, leaving IgM preserved or elevated while switched isotypes are reduced.
Source Section: Immunodeficiency Syndromes - hyper-IgM syndrome; PDF p. 50
Notes: Verified: CD40LG (CD40L) deficiency impairs class-switch recombination; normal/elevated IgM with low IgG/IgA/IgE (Bonilla et al., JACI 2015). Title correctly specifies the CD40L subtype (other causes: AID, CD40, NEMO).

Explanation: STAT3-related hyper-IgE syndrome combines a characteristic immune defect with eczema, high IgE and recurrent abscesses that may show little overt inflammation.
Source Section: Immunodeficiency Syndromes - Job syndrome; PDF p. 50
Notes: Verified: autosomal dominant STAT3 loss-of-function (Job) syndrome - eczema, cold (non-inflamed) abscesses, very high IgE (Bonilla et al., JACI 2015). Qualifier: distinct from DOCK8 deficiency; cold abscesses characteristic, not mandatory.

Explanation: WAS protein dysfunction produces an immune deficiency classically accompanied by eczema and microthrombocytopenia.
Source Section: Immunodeficiency Syndromes - Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome; PDF p. 50
Notes: Verified: WAS gene defect, triad of eczema, (micro)thrombocytopenia with small platelets, recurrent infection (Bonilla et al., JACI 2015). 'Small platelets' reflects the classic untreated pattern.

Explanation: Each named gene-related disorder has X-linked inheritance; the qualifiers prevent extrapolation to unrelated causes of similar phenotypes.
Source Section: Immunodeficiency Syndromes - inheritance and gene defects; PDF pp. 49-52
Notes: Verified X-linked inheritance: BTK (XLA), CD40LG (X-linked hyper-IgM), WAS, FOXP3 (IPEX) (Bonilla et al., JACI 2015; Lu et al., Nat Rev Immunol 2017). Board overlap: these disease tiles duplicate clue groups IMM-022/025/027 - never place on the same 16-tile board.

Tile 4: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
Explanation: Antibodies directed against blood-cell antigens cause immune destruction of erythrocytes or platelets in these classic type II hypersensitivity examples.
Source Section: Hypersensitivity Reactions - type II destructive mechanism; PDF p. 56
Notes: Verified antibody-mediated (type II) cytopenias (Chapel and Haeney 2023; Uzzaman and Cho, Allergy Asthma Proc 2012).

Explanation: Antigen-antibody complexes drive tissue inflammation in these type III examples; the lupus tile specifies immune-complex renal disease rather than all manifestations of SLE.
Source Section: Hypersensitivity Reactions - type III mechanism, serum sickness and Arthus; PDF pp. 57, 59
Notes: Verified immune-complex (type III) diseases (Chapel and Haeney 2023). Lupus nephritis is explicitly qualified as the immune-complex manifestation. Do not substitute 'serum sickness-like reaction.'

Explanation: These reactions depend on antigen-specific T-cell responses rather than an immediate IgE-mediated process; the skin tests assess delayed cellular reactivity.
Source Section: Hypersensitivity Reactions - type IV diagnostics and skin differential; PDF p. 58
Notes: Verified delayed-type (type IV) reactions (Chapel and Haeney 2023; Uzzaman and Cho 2012). Qualifier: 'Candida' tile = delayed recall skin test, not candidal infection - retain this wording to avoid ambiguity.

Explanation: Immune destruction of red cells produces a positive direct antiglobulin test with elevated LDH and indirect bilirubin and low haptoglobin; this pattern applies to immune hemolysis generally, including transfusion-related and autoimmune causes.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Immune hemolysis laboratory pattern; autoimmune hemolytic anemia labs
Source Section: Transfusion Reactions - acute and delayed hemolytic reactions; PDF pp. 62-63
Notes: REVISED: title broadened from 'immune transfusion hemolysis' to 'immune-mediated hemolysis' because the four-marker pattern is not transfusion-specific. Competing category: autoimmune hemolytic anemia fits equally (standard hematology references, e.g., Brodsky, Blood 2014). Qualifier: DAT can be negative in some immune hemolysis; do not present as transfusion-specific or diagnostic in isolation.

Explanation: TRALI involves acute inflammatory pulmonary injury following transfusion, with capillary leak and noncardiogenic edema rather than hydrostatic volume overload.
Source Section: Transfusion Reactions - transfusion-related acute lung injury; PDF p. 65
Notes: Verified: noncardiogenic pulmonary edema from neutrophil-mediated increased permeability, new bilateral infiltrates within 6h of transfusion (Soutar et al., Br J Haematol 2023). Qualifier: distinguish from TACO (hydrostatic); donor antibodies are not always detectable.

Explanation: Preformed recipient antibodies recognizing donor antigens can cause rapid vascular injury, thrombosis and ischemic graft destruction.
Source Section: Transplant Rejection - hyperacute rejection; PDF p. 71
Notes: Verified: preformed recipient anti-donor (ABO/HLA) antibodies cause within-minutes microvascular thrombosis and fibrinoid necrosis (Suthanthiran and Strom, NEJM 1994;331:365).

Explanation: Chronic rejection is associated with progressive vascular narrowing, fibrosis and loss of graft tissue over time.
Source Section: Transplant Rejection - chronic rejection; PDF p. 73
Notes: Verified: graft vasculopathy/arteriosclerosis, intimal smooth-muscle proliferation, interstitial fibrosis, parenchymal atrophy (Suthanthiran and Strom, NEJM 1994). Qualifier: morphology varies by transplanted organ; findings are supportive, not each individually required.

Explanation: Immunocompetent donor T cells may injure recipient skin, gut and liver after transplantation, producing the classic GVHD pattern.
Source Section: Transplant Rejection - graft-versus-host disease; PDF p. 74
Notes: Verified: donor T cells attack host skin (rash), gut (diarrhea), liver (cholestatic jaundice) (Chapel and Haeney 2023). Classic syndrome pattern, not a required 4-part checklist.

Connection Title: Drugs inhibiting IL-2 production or signaling
Explanation: Cyclosporine and tacrolimus reduce IL-2 transcription through calcineurin inhibition; sirolimus inhibits mTOR downstream of IL-2 signaling, and basiliximab blocks CD25, the IL-2 receptor alpha chain.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Inhibitors along the IL-2 activation pathway
Source Section: Transplant Rejection - immunosuppressive pharmacology; PDF p. 76
Notes: Verified (Halloran, NEJM 2004;351:2715; Schrezenmeier et al., Transplantation 2024, PMID 37309030): calcineurin inhibitors block IL-2 transcription, sirolimus blocks mTOR downstream of IL-2R, basiliximab targets CD25 (IL-2Ralpha). Category correctly spans IL-2 production and signaling, not calcineurin alone.

Explanation: Systemic glucocorticoid exposure can cause each of these adverse effects; likelihood depends on dose, duration and individual susceptibility.
Source Section: Transplant Rejection - glucocorticoids; PDF p. 77
Notes: Verified dose/duration-dependent adverse effects: osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, iatrogenic Cushing syndrome, avascular necrosis of the femoral head (standard pharmacology references, e.g., Katzung, Basic and Clinical Pharmacology 15e, 2021). 'Can occur,' not universal.

Explanation: These biologics neutralize TNF-alpha signaling. Certolizumab is a pegylated antigen-binding fragment; the relationship does not require all four to be intact antibodies.
Source Section: Transplant Rejection - TNF inhibitors; PDF p. 78
Notes: Verified TNF-alpha inhibitors (FDA labels; standard pharmacology references). Certolizumab is a PEGylated Fab' (no Fc) - a title requiring four intact monoclonal antibodies would be incorrect. Etanercept (TNF-receptor fusion protein) is a defensible alternate TNF inhibitor if a substitute is ever needed.
